Boyle and Jenner Launch London Arts Project for Working-Class and LGBTQ Youth

Danny Boyle and Caitlyn Jenner stood together in Leicester Square on Tuesday to launch "Square One," a London-based arts and media initiative that, after months of talks with youth charities, local councils and entertainment companies, will pair Steve Jones and Paul Cook with LGBTQ advocates, young actors and reality-television producers in a yearlong effort to help working-class teenagers turn personal stories into music, short films and digital programs, with financial backing and distribution commitments from Disney+, Hulu and E!.

Organizers said the program will begin this autumn with free workshops in rehearsal rooms off King's Road, where selected participants from across Britain will study songwriting, live performance, camera work, editing, media law and public speaking before pitching original projects about identity, family pressure, housing insecurity and the cost-of-living crisis, with travel stipends and meal support included so that applicants are not filtered out simply because they cannot afford repeated journeys into central London.

Boyle, who will direct a feature-length documentary following the first group of students from auditions to public performances, said he wanted to build something less polished than a conventional talent competition and more rooted in the restless energy that once made London's youth culture feel capable of confronting social hierarchies, adding that the point was not to manufacture instant stars but to give young people the technical confidence and institutional access that are usually reserved for those who already know how the industry works.

Jenner, joining as an executive producer and one of several public mentors, said the reality-television component commissioned by E! would focus not on celebrity spectacle but on how young people navigate public attention when private questions about gender, class, family expectations and belonging suddenly become content for audiences, advertisers and social media platforms, a process she said can be empowering for some participants but destabilizing for others unless they are given legal advice, counseling and meaningful editorial say over how their stories are told.

Jones and Cook, announced as music leads for the project, told reporters they plan to emphasize rehearsal discipline as much as attitude, saying participants will be expected to write original material and perform live at a series of neighborhood showcases rather than rely on backing tracks or image-making alone, with the strongest songs and stage concepts feeding into a finale scheduled for Leicester Square next spring that organizers hope will draw record labels, independent promoters, school groups and community arts networks.

The initiative has also secured the involvement of several fashion and film figures connected to King's Road, including designers working with archives associated with Vivienne Westwood, who will help students build stage looks from recycled and donated materials, while cinematographers and production designers will run weekend sessions on low-budget visual storytelling so that those interested in directing or costume work are not treated as secondary to performers, an approach Boyle said reflects the fact that cultural movements are usually shaped backstage as much as they are in front of microphones.

Disney+ will distribute Boyle's documentary in Britain and parts of Europe, Hulu will carry it in the United States, and executives involved in the agreement said the streaming rollout is designed to connect British youth arts groups with American nonprofits that have expanded services for transgender people and low-income young adults, while also creating a revenue pool that organizers say will be ringfenced for bursaries, emergency housing referrals, mental-health counseling and small grants for participants who want to keep developing their work after the cameras stop rolling.

A separate eight-part unscripted series for E! is expected to enter production later this summer, following selected participants as they move from small audition rooms to larger stages and discover how contracts, sponsorships, magazine profiles and online commentary can alter friendships and family dynamics when unfamiliar levels of visibility begin to look financially transformative, a theme producers said would be handled with slower pacing and more off-camera support than is common in entertainment formats built around conflict.

City officials backing the plan said the partnership could bring new foot traffic to central London venues still rebuilding audiences after years of economic strain, and several schools, youth theaters and community centers have already asked for places after hearing that applicants will receive training from drummers, vocal coaches, camera operators, editors, publicists and welfare advisers rather than being limited to a single discipline, with organizers setting aside a portion of admissions for teenagers referred by shelters and social workers.

Not everyone is convinced that a project involving major entertainment brands can preserve its grassroots promise, and some campaigners warned that stories about transition, poverty or social exclusion can easily be flattened into marketable narratives, but Boyle argued that wide distribution is precisely what gives teenagers from overlooked neighborhoods a realistic chance to be heard, while Jenner said commercial success and social understanding do not have to be enemies if participants retain control over their names, images, contracts and the terms on which they tell deeply personal experiences.

Applications open next week, with the first cohort set to start in September, and organizers said the launch concert will raise money for London youth shelters, community centers and emergency arts funds, with Jones describing that outcome as the point of the whole venture because talent, however rebellious, vulnerable or unconventional, too often disappears when young people cannot afford rehearsal space, safe housing, decent transport or simply enough time away from low-paid work to discover what they might become.

UAA Plans Anchorage-Brighton Arts Forum on Free Expression

The University of Alaska Anchorage said on Tuesday that it would stage a weeklong transatlantic arts forum this spring, pairing a new exhibition by assistant professor Thomas Chung with performances by singer-songwriter Nadia Reid, Welsh composer Meilyr Jones, British vocalist Eska Mtungwazi and Irish electronic musician Jack Colleran, in an effort to test how a public university can present forceful art while still making room for parents, students and taxpayers who dislike what they see and hear. The program, titled Common Ground Sessions, will begin at the Kimora Gallery inside the Fine Arts building before shifting to evening events shared with the Sallis Benney theatre in Brighton through a live digital link, a format organizers said was designed to connect Alaska audiences with a British venue known for intimate performances and to give artists a chance to address the same questions about expression, civics and institutional responsibility in two sharply different cultural settings. Steven Godfrey, chairman of UAA's Fine Arts Department, said the idea emerged after faculty discussions about whether universities too often defend creative freedom in theory but fail to provide a disciplined public setting in which critics of challenging work can question artists directly, ask how public money is being spent and hear why a piece that feels abrasive or unsettling may still belong in an academic environment.

Under the plan, Chung will present a newly commissioned installation combining student paintings, projected fragments of song lyrics, classroom notes and recorded testimony from Anchorage residents, while Reid, Jones, Eska and Colleran will each perform short sets followed by moderated conversations about authorship, emotional risk and the difference between art that invites argument and art that merely seeks attention, with the university promising that audience members will be able to submit written questions and speak from floor microphones. Chung, who was born in New Jersey, grew up in Hong Kong and New York City, and later earned degrees from the San Francisco Art Institute and Yale University, said he agreed to take part only after organizers accepted his insistence that the event should not become a civility exercise in which artists are pressed to dilute their convictions, even as he also pushed for clear ground rules that would keep personal attacks and partisan chanting out of the room. Advance images released by UAA show that Chung's work will avoid portraits of elected officials and instead layer photographs of empty lecture halls, two amplified eagle calls and handwritten reflections from students about fear, belonging and patriotism, a choice he said was meant to redirect attention from personalities toward the more durable question of how national language enters classrooms, galleries and family conversations when political temperatures rise.

Paul Berger, a former adjunct professor who was invited onto a community advisory panel after years of speaking about children's exposure to challenging material in publicly supported venues, said he appreciated the university's decision to publish age guidance, hold afternoon rehearsals open to families and make the curatorial statement available in advance, but remained doubtful that an event financed partly with state funds could avoid sliding from cultural exploration into one-sided advocacy. Reid and Jones, in written comments distributed by the organizers, said campus audiences tend to listen more patiently than festival crowds and often ask sharper questions about craft, while Eska described the Anchorage residency as an opportunity to see whether an intimate room could sustain disagreement without losing its sense of wonder, and Colleran said he planned to build his closing performance from audience recordings gathered during workshops on memory, noise, speech and the fraying edges of sound. The workshops will also include sessions for local teachers, who are being offered lesson plans on free expression, the responsibilities of public institutions and the history of works that were initially rejected by communities before being reconsidered as serious cultural statements, a move UAA officials said could help schools prepare older students for a forum likely to move quickly from aesthetic judgment to broader questions about citizenship and dissent.

Reaction on campus was divided after the announcement, with some students praising the administration for refusing to treat controversy as a reason to retreat from difficult programming and others questioning why the university was bringing in overseas performers during a tight budget year, prompting officials to say that most travel, technical and housing costs were being met by private donors, ticket sales and British partners rather than by general tuition revenue. By Wednesday afternoon, the first night's seats were nearly gone, a result organizers attributed partly to curiosity about the unusual mix of folk songwriting, theatrical pop, experimental electronics and visual art, and partly to a public mood in Anchorage that has grown weary of online quarrels and may be more open to events where disagreement unfolds slowly, under lights and in front of neighbors, instead of through anonymous posts and clipped slogans. Common Ground Sessions will remain in Anchorage through April 20 before the final discussion is carried back to Brighton, where the Sallis Benney theatre audience will be asked to respond to material generated in Alaska, and Godfrey said the experiment would count as a success not if everyone left impressed or persuaded, but if people who arrived expecting offense stayed long enough to wrestle seriously with artists whose work unsettled them.
